activities.caption: find the line the speed-myth would love
activities.name: nnCeilingSpot

config.prompt: One line of this study plan contradicts the research — click it:
lines: Native listening runs at two to three words per second.
There is plenty of time to consciously translate each phrase as it arrives.
Comprehension must therefore run on recognition, built by massive input.
Shadowing forces perception up to native speed; dictation trains precision.
Humour is the hardest input — jokes depend on shared scripts and timing.
config.correction: At that speed nothing keeps up except recognition — no time for translation at all.
config.why: The remaining gap at this tier is coverage, not grammar — regional accents, fast colloquial speech, professional registers, literature, humour — closed by register-specific volume.

activities.anchor: (Spanish, French, Dutch) are budgeted at roughly 600–750
activities.caption: call the bill — the hardest category
activities.name: nnFsiEstimate

config.prompt: The FSI's hardest category — Mandarin, Arabic, Japanese, Korean — allots roughly how many classroom hours to professional working proficiency?
config.why: About 2,200 — and near-native performance exceeds professional working proficiency by a wide margin, so expert-tier command costs several thousand hours spread across registers. Input volume is the load-bearing variable: every serious method at this tier is a delivery system for input, not a better mnemonic.
config.context: The easy categories reach working proficiency for a fraction of that — and this tier aims well beyond working proficiency.

config.prompt: Word families for comfortable, unassisted reading of ordinary text — where does Nation's threshold sit?
config.why: Roughly 8,000–9,000 for text; speech manages with 6,000–7,000, because it runs on a smaller, more repetitive store while writing carries the rare words. Past the line, acquisition switches from meeting to harvesting — frequency lists, spaced retrieval, extensive reading.
config.context: A near-native listener is one whose store crossed the line where guessing from context becomes reliable.

activities.anchor: note-taking systems for oral input (interpreters' symbol-and-structure method)
activities.caption: line up the mediation pipeline
activities.name: nnMediationOrder

config.prompt: Mediation's mechanism — order the pipeline, first step first:
items: Take in multi-source material — a debate, a report, a conversation
Hold the propositional content while the speaker runs on
Rebuild it in the target language's own discourse architecture
config.why: Discourse markers and connectives are the cohesion skeleton that makes reconstruction sound native; the ladder — same-language paraphrase, written summary from memory, consecutive delivery — trains each move under pressure.

activities.caption: drag the divider — myth, then craft
activities.name: nnInterpCompare

config.prompt: One job, two pictures of it — drag the divider:

before.label: The myth
before.text: Word-for-word at speed: follow the source's syntax like a guide and render each word as it lands.

after.label: The craft
after.text: Deverbalise: drop the wording, hold the content through a managed lag of a few seconds while the speaker runs on. The source's syntax is a trap, not a guide — the notes are arrows, never sentences.

config.why: Employers probe this first: near-native speakers are hired to be bridges, and bridging is a distinct competence from fluent conversation.

activities.caption: file each fix under its home
activities.name: nnShadesBuckets

config.prompt: The finer shades of meaning — file each fix under the layer it serves:

items.label: multi-word chunks like native-like "heavy rain", never word-by-word assembly
reading across registers until formal, informal, technical and diplomatic phrasing comes by default
self-recording with an error log and counts
deliberate practice with immediate correction on stable old errors
prosody first — rhythm and intonation carry more accent than phonemes — plus phonetic coaching
how far to assimilate the accent at all

config.why: Stable old errors survive because ordinary input no longer notices them — Selinker's fossilisation (1972): stable errors in an otherwise advancing interlanguage. Intelligibility and register control are the functional goals; a marked accent is identity, not failure.

activities.anchor: separates three things that get conflated
activities.caption: pair each term with its meaning
activities.name: nnIntelligMatch

config.prompt: Munro and Derwing's programme — pair each construct with its definition:

pairs.right: how hard you are to understand
comprehensibility and intelligibility — degree of foreign accent barely does

config.why: A clearly accented speaker with full register control outperforms a native-sounding one who misses pragmatic cues — the profession's own hierarchy, priced in hiring.

activities.anchor: the L1 is a resource, not a contaminant
activities.caption: design the term's schedule
activities.name: nnScheduleBranch

config.root: Design this term's schedule for an adult aiming at the expert tier.

start.text: How do you treat the first language?

choices.label: Ban it entirely — total monolingual immersion
choices.feedback: You buy processing practice — and pay with the metalinguistic leverage adults uniquely possess.

choices.label: Keep everything bilingual
choices.feedback: Conceptual foundations transfer and contrast exposes what the new language does differently — but automaticity never arrives without input-dense practice.

ban.text: Classroom research on planned bilingual use (translanguaging) generally favours it over strict bans for vocabulary growth.

choices.label: Rebuild the schedule
choices.feedback: You can buy the practice without paying the ban's cost.

bilingual.text: What immersion adds is irreplaceable processing practice — comprehension at native speed is bought only with volume.

choices.label: Rebuild the schedule
choices.feedback: Add input-dense blocks; keep the contrast work.

both.text: Input-dense immersion for automaticity, bilingual contrast for precision — scheduled together, not traded off.

config.why: The first language is leverage; the immersion block is practice — the expert's schedule uses both on purpose.
